title: 4_Projectile Motion

findings.finding: Connect the component magnitudes with the projectile's minimum speed.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects the zero vertical component at the apex with the magnitude formula.
findings.checked: p3-definition-block establishes constant horizontal velocity; p4-diagram-components shows zero vertical velocity at the apex. The proposed answers follow from speed = sqrt(64 + vertical velocity squared).
findings.assumptions: The projectile was launched upwards and reaches its apex during the modelled flight.

repair.proposal: Append to p5-magnitude-activity-block: (c) The projectile in part a was launched upwards. Find its velocity components at the highest point. Answer: horizontal 8 m/s, vertical 0 m/s. (d) Find its speed there. Answer: 8 m/s. (e) Explain why its speed cannot fall below 8 m/s during flight. Answer: its horizontal component remains 8 m/s and its speed is sqrt(64 + vertical velocity squared), which is at least 8 m/s.

findings.doneWhen: The added parts use part a's projectile to connect its components with its minimum speed.

findings.finding: The opening review does not rehearse linear solving and common-factor quadratic solving used to find flight times.
findings.breakdown: p14-example-b requires solving a linear equation; p14-example-d requires factorisation and the zero-product rule before selecting the landing root.
findings.checked: The preceding topic rehearses integration, initial conditions and vector notation, but neither its teaching nor supplied practice rehearses these equation-solving methods. p13-identify selects equations without solving them. These are substantial algebraic steps, rather than final simplifications.
findings.assumptions: These are prior Stage 6 algebra skills. Calculator availability does not change the missing rehearsal.

repair.proposal: Before p12-maximum-height, add three short review items: (a) Solve -10t+15=0. Answer: t=1.5. (b) Factorise -5t²+20t. Answer: -5t(t-4). (c) Solve -5t²+10√2t=0, giving both solutions. Answer: t=0 or t=2√2.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse linear solving, common-factor factorisation and the zero-product rule before the flight-feature examples.

findings.finding: Compare the complementary-angle launches with a launch at 45° using the same speed.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up exposes how changing the launch angle changes range while speed remains fixed.
findings.checked: For V=20 and g=10, the 45° launch has flight time 2√2 s and range 40 m. The existing launches each have range 20√3 m. All required methods appear in this topic.
findings.assumptions: The third stone returns to the same ground level, under the existing projectile model.

repair.proposal: After p20-q12-b add: (c) A third stone is thrown from the same point at 20 m/s at 45° above the horizontal. Find its time of flight. Answer: 2√2 s. (d) Find its range. Answer: 40 m. (e) How much farther does it land than either of the first two stones? Give an exact answer and an answer to 1 d.p. Answer: 40-20√3 m, approximately 5.4 m.

findings.doneWhen: The existing comparison includes a numerical 45° launch using the same speed and launch point.

findings.finding: Vary cliff height while holding horizontal launch speed fixed.
findings.breakdown: The sequence exposes the square-root dependence of flight time and range on drop height.
findings.checked: With g=10 and horizontal speed 2, heights 5, 20, 45 and 80 m give ranges 2, 4, 6 and 8 m. The unpatterned case gives 3√2 m. The supplied practice contains no equivalent consecutive comparison.
findings.assumptions: Water leaves each cliff horizontally; the section's g=10 m/s² instruction applies.

repair.proposal: Make the existing p25-q2 task part (a). Add one instruction: “Predict how the distance changes before calculating.” Add further parts under the same waterfall instruction: (b) cliff height 20 m, speed 2 m/s; answer 4 m. (c) cliff height 45 m, speed 2 m/s; answer 6 m. (d) cliff height 80 m, speed 2 m/s; answer 8 m. (e) cliff height 10 m, speed 3 m/s; answer 3√2 m, approximately 4.2 m. Place before p25-q3.

findings.doneWhen: The original case and three added cases vary only height, followed by one unpatterned case.

findings.finding: The shared method for an unknown “angle or speed” directs every case to a quadratic in tanθ, including the known-angle task p36-q1.
findings.breakdown: Following step 3 directs students to solve for the given angle rather than the unknown speed.
findings.checked: Eliminating time in p36-q1 gives 1000=2000√3-80000000/V², which must be solved for positive V. p35-example-demonstration models only an unknown angle. Earlier teaching does not correct the shared instruction's endpoint.
findings.assumptions: Students apply the numbered instructions to both cases explicitly named in their introduction.

repair.proposal: Replace step 3 in p35-teaching with: “If the angle is unknown, use sec²θ=1+tan²θ to obtain a quadratic in tanθ. If the angle is known and the speed is unknown, substitute the angle and solve the resulting equation for V, taking the positive speed.”

findings.doneWhen: The shared method provides a correct endpoint for both unknown-angle and unknown-speed tasks.

findings.finding: Compare the speeds of the two trajectories at another common height.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up extends the existing comparison of velocities at P to distinguish equal speed from differing directions.
findings.checked: Both trajectories reach 20 m: their maximum heights are 25 m and approximately 119.1 m. Substitution into the taught component equations gives speed sqrt(2500-400)=10√21, approximately 45.8 m/s, for each trajectory. No energy method is required.

repair.proposal: After p39-q5-b-ii add (c): “For each angle of projection, find the speed when the particle first reaches 20 m above its launch point. Give your answers to 1 decimal place.” Answer: 45.8 m/s for each angle.

findings.doneWhen: The added part compares both trajectories at the same new height using existing methods.

findings.finding: p45-q1 repeats the complete mathematical task in p44-q1 without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: The path and all three requested features are unchanged, allowing the guided-practice results to be reproduced.
findings.checked: Compared both complete tasks: each gives y=x/2-x²/160 and asks for projection angle, range and maximum height. The rounding instruction does not change the underlying task. No instructional purpose for repetition is stated. For the replacement, the positive root is 96, the vertex is (48,18), and arctan(3/4) rounds to 36.9°.
findings.assumptions: Guided practice precedes the exercise in the supplied order.

repair.proposal: Replace the path in p45-q1 with y=3x/4-x²/128 and retain its three parts. Answers: (a) 36.9° above the horizontal; (b) 96 units; (c) 18 units.

findings.doneWhen: The later copy retains its structure but uses a different path and requires fresh calculations.
